answer:
Given: \(\log_{10}\left(\frac{x^{3} - y^{3}}{x^{3} + y^{3}}\right) = 2\)

Writing the logarithmic equation in exponential form,
\(\frac{x^{3} - y^{3}}{x^{3} + y^{3}} = 10^{2} = 100\)
\(\therefore x^{3} - y^{3} = 100x^{3} + 100y^{3}\)
\(\therefore -99x^{3} = 101y^{3}\)

This relation is free of logarithms. Differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\),
\(-99 \cdot 3x^{2} = 101 \cdot 3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}\)
\(\therefore -297x^{2} = 303y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{297x^{2}}{303y^{2}}\)

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by \(3\),
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{99x^{2}}{101y^{2}}\), as required.

[The whole trick is to clear the logarithm FIRST. Differentiating \(\log_{10}\) of a quotient directly also works, but it needs the quotient rule inside a log and is far longer.]

Let \(y = x^{x}\).

The base and the index both contain \(x\), so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies directly. Take \(\log\) of both sides,
\(\log y = \log x^{x} = x\log x\)

Differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\) (product rule on the right),
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\log x) + \log x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(x)\)
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{1}{x} + \log x\cdot 1 = 1 + \log x\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = y\left(1 + \log x\right)\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = x^{x}\left(1 + \log x\right)\), for \(x > 0\).

Check: at \(x = 1\) this gives \(1^{1}(1 + 0) = 1\), which is the slope of \(y = x^{x}\) at \((1, 1)\).

Let \(y = \cos^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\right)\)

The \(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) is the \(\sin 2\theta\) pattern, so substitute
\(x = \sin\theta\), \(\therefore \theta = \sin^{-1}x\)
\(\therefore y = \cos^{-1}\left(2\sin\theta\sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\theta}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\right)\)
\(y = \cos^{-1}(\sin 2\theta)\)
\(y = \cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\theta\right)\right] = \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\theta\)
\(\therefore y = \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\sin^{-1}x\)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - 2\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^{-1}x\right) = 0 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\)

[Range note, stated because the substitution hides it: the step \(\cos^{-1}[\cos(\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\theta)] = \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\theta\) needs \(0 \leq \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\theta \leq \pi\), i.e. \(-\frac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{4}\), i.e. \(|x| \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). For \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < |x| < 1\) the same working gives \(+\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\) (checked numerically at \(x = 0.9\)). The board expects the principal-range answer above.]

Given: \(x\sin y + y\sin x = 0\)

Here \(y\) cannot be written explicitly in terms of \(x\), so differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\) and using the product rule on each term,
\(\frac{d}{dx}(x\sin y) + \frac{d}{dx}(y\sin x) = 0\)
\(\left[x\cos y\frac{dy}{dx} + \sin y\cdot 1\right] + \left[\sin x\frac{dy}{dx} + y\cos x\right] = 0\)

Collecting the \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) terms on one side,
\((x\cos y + \sin x)\frac{dy}{dx} = -\left(\sin y + y\cos x\right)\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{\sin y + y\cos x}{x\cos y + \sin x}\), provided \(x\cos y + \sin x \neq 0\).

Let \(y = \tan^{2}\left(\log x^{3}\right)\), i.e. \(y = \left[\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\right]^{2}\), where \(x > 0\).

This is a composite of three functions (square of tan of log), so differentiate w. r. t. \(x\) by the chain rule, peeling one layer at a time.
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\right]\)
\(= 2\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\cdot\sec^{2}\left(\log x^{3}\right)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\log x^{3}\right)\)

Now \(\log x^{3} = 3\log x\), so \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\log x^{3}\right) = 3\cdot\frac{1}{x} = \frac{3}{x}\).

\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = 2\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\cdot\sec^{2}\left(\log x^{3}\right)\cdot\frac{3}{x}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{6}{x}\tan\left(\log x^{3}\right)\sec^{2}\left(\log x^{3}\right)\)

Let \(y = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5x + 1}{3 - x - 6x^{2}}\right)\)

Differentiating this directly is very heavy. Instead force the stem into the form \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{A + B}{1 - AB}\right) = \tan^{-1}A + \tan^{-1}B\).

Write the denominator as \(1\) minus something:
\(3 - x - 6x^{2} = 1 + 2 - x - 6x^{2} = 1 - \left(6x^{2} + x - 2\right)\)
Factorise \(6x^{2} + x - 2 = 6x^{2} + 4x - 3x - 2 = 2x(3x + 2) - (3x + 2) = (3x + 2)(2x - 1)\)
\(\therefore 3 - x - 6x^{2} = 1 - (3x + 2)(2x - 1)\)

And the numerator splits to match: \((3x + 2) + (2x - 1) = 5x + 1\).

\(\therefore y = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{(3x + 2) + (2x - 1)}{1 - (3x + 2)(2x - 1)}\right)\)
\(\therefore y = \tan^{-1}(3x + 2) + \tan^{-1}(2x - 1)\)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{1 + (3x + 2)^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(3x + 2) + \frac{1}{1 + (2x - 1)^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(2x - 1)\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3}{1 + (3x + 2)^{2}} + \frac{2}{1 + (2x - 1)^{2}}\)

[Verified: differentiating the original expression directly gives the same function.]

Let \(y = x^{x}\).

The base and the index both contain \(x\), so take \(\log\) of both sides,
\(\log y = \log x^{x} = x\log x\)

Differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\) (product rule on the right),
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{1}{x} + \log x\cdot 1 = 1 + \log x\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = y\left(1 + \log x\right)\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = x^{x}\left(1 + \log x\right)\), for \(x > 0\).

[The identical question was set in March 2016; \(x^{x}\) is the standard test of logarithmic differentiation.]

Let \(y = \sin\left(x^{2} + x\right)\).

This is \(\sin\) of a function of \(x\), so differentiate by the chain rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \cos\left(x^{2} + x\right)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2} + x\right)\)
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \cos\left(x^{2} + x\right)\cdot(2x + 1)\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = (2x + 1)\cos\left(x^{2} + x\right)\)

Let \(y = \log(\sec x + \tan x)\).

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\) by the chain rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sec x + \tan x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x + \tan x)\)
\(= \frac{\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x}{\sec x + \tan x}\)

Take \(\sec x\) common in the numerator,
\(= \frac{\sec x\left(\tan x + \sec x\right)}{\sec x + \tan x}\)

The bracket cancels with the denominator,
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \sec x\)

[This is worth remembering: \(\log(\sec x + \tan x)\) is an antiderivative of \(\sec x\), which is where the integral \(\int\sec x\,dx\) comes from.]

**(D)** \(1\)

First find \(y\) when \(x = 0\). Putting \(x = 0\) in \(\log(x + y) = 2xy\),
\(\log(0 + y) = 0\) \(\therefore \log y = 0\) \(\therefore y = 1\).

Now differentiate \(\log(x + y) = 2xy\) w. r. t. \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\) (chain rule on the left, product rule on the right),
\(\frac{1}{x + y}\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 2\left(y + x\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\)

Substitute \(x = 0\), \(y = 1\),
\(\frac{1 + y'}{0 + 1} = 2\left(1 + 0\right)\)
\(1 + y' = 2\)
\(\therefore y'(0) = 1\)
twin: If \(y\) is a function of \(x\) and \(\log(x + y) = 2xy\), then the value of \(y'(0) = \) ...

answer:
The radical is self-similar: everything under the outermost square root, after the \(\tan x\), is the whole expression \(y\) over again. So

\(y = \sqrt{\tan x + y}\)

Squaring both sides turns it into an implicit relation between \(x\) and \(y\):

\(y^{2} = \tan x + y\)

Differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), remembering that \(y\) is a function of \(x\):

\(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sec^{2}x + \dfrac{dy}{dx}\)

\(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sec^{2}x\)

\((2y - 1)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sec^{2}x\)

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2y - 1}\)

which is the required result.

**Value of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x = 0\).**

Solving \(y^{2} - y - \tan x = 0\) as a quadratic in \(y\):

\(y = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4\tan x}}{2}\)

The nested radical is a square root, so \(y \geq 0\), and for \(\tan x > 0\) the value it converges to is the branch with the plus sign:

\(y = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\tan x}}{2}\)

Letting \(x \to 0\) along this branch,

\(y \to \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 0}}{2} = \dfrac{1 + 1}{2} = 1\)

**Convention stated explicitly, because the answer turns on it:** at \(x = 0\) the relation \(y^{2} = y\) also has the root \(y = 0\). That is the isolated degenerate root, not the value traced by the branch the expression follows for \(x\) near 0, and it is discarded; taking it instead would give \(-1\). The value used here is \(y = 1\).

Therefore

\(\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x = 0} = \dfrac{\sec^{2}0}{2(1) - 1} = \dfrac{1^{2}}{1} = 1\)
twin: If \(y = \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \ldots \infty}}}\), then show that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sec^2 x}{2y - 1}\).

answer:
Let \(y = (\log x)^{x}\).

The index is \(x\) and the base contains \(x\), so take \(\log\) of both sides,
\(\log y = \log\left[(\log x)^{x}\right] = x\log(\log x)\)

Differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\) (product rule on the right, chain rule inside \(\log(\log x)\)),
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\cdot\log(\log x) + x\cdot\frac{1}{\log x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\log x)\)
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \log(\log x) + x\cdot\frac{1}{\log x}\cdot\frac{1}{x}\)
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \log(\log x) + \frac{1}{\log x}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = (\log x)^{x}\left[\log(\log x) + \frac{1}{\log x}\right]\)

(Valid where \(\log x > 0\), i.e. \(x > 1\), so that \(\log(\log x)\) is defined.)

**(D)**

Let \(h(x) = \sqrt{\left[f(x)\right]^{2} + \left[g(x)\right]^{2}}\).

Put \(u = \left[f(x)\right]^{2} + \left[g(x)\right]^{2}\), so \(h = \sqrt{u}\). By the chain rule,

\(h'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}\)

and \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2f(x)f'(x) + 2g(x)g'(x)\), so

\(h'(x) = \dfrac{2f(x)f'(x) + 2g(x)g'(x)}{2\sqrt{\left[f(x)\right]^{2} + \left[g(x)\right]^{2}}} = \dfrac{f(x)f'(x) + g(x)g'(x)}{\sqrt{\left[f(x)\right]^{2} + \left[g(x)\right]^{2}}}\)

Now substitute the values at \(x = 1\):

\(f(1)f'(1) = 3 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -1\)

\(g(1)g'(1) = (-4) \times \left(-\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{32}{3}\)

Numerator \(= -1 + \dfrac{32}{3} = \dfrac{-3 + 32}{3} = \dfrac{29}{3}\)

Denominator \(= \sqrt{3^{2} + (-4)^{2}} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\)

\(h'(1) = \dfrac{\dfrac{29}{3}}{5} = \dfrac{29}{15}\)

which is option (D).

Note the sign trap the paper sets: \(f'(1) = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), NOT \(+\dfrac{1}{3}\). Taking it positive gives \(1 + \dfrac{32}{3} = \dfrac{35}{3}\), and \(\dfrac{35}{3} \div 5 = \dfrac{7}{3}\) — which is option (B), printed on the paper as a distractor for exactly that slip.

Given: \(y = \left(\tan^{-1}x\right)^{2}\) ... (I)

Differentiate (I) w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\tan^{-1}x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}x\right) = \frac{2\tan^{-1}x}{1 + x^{2}}\)

Clear the denominator before differentiating again — that keeps the second step short:
\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\tan^{-1}x\) ... (II)

Differentiate (II) w. r. t. \(x\), using the product rule on the left,
\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot 2x = \frac{2}{1 + x^{2}}\)

Multiply throughout by \(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\),
\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)^{2}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 2x\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\)

Hence the result. [Verified independently by direct computation of \(y_{1}\) and \(y_{2}\): the left side simplifies to the constant \(2\).]
twin: If \(y = e^{m \tan^{-1} x}\), show that \((1 + x^2) \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + (2x - m) \frac{dy}{dx} = 0\)

answer:
Let \(y = x\log x\), \(x > 0\).

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\) by the product rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\log x) + \log x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(x)\)
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{1}{x} + \log x\cdot 1\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \log x\)

Differentiate again w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(1 + \log x\right) = 0 + \frac{1}{x}\)
\(\therefore \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{1}{x}\)

Given: \(e^{x} + e^{y} = e^{x + y}\) ... (I)

Differentiate both sides w. r. t. \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\),
\(e^{x} + e^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x + y}\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right)\)
\(\therefore e^{x} + e^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x + y} + e^{x + y}\frac{dy}{dx}\)

Collecting the \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) terms,
\(\left(e^{y} - e^{x + y}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x + y} - e^{x}\)

Now use the given relation (I), i.e. \(e^{x + y} = e^{x} + e^{y}\), on both sides:
Numerator: \(e^{x + y} - e^{x} = \left(e^{x} + e^{y}\right) - e^{x} = e^{y}\)
Denominator: \(e^{y} - e^{x + y} = e^{y} - \left(e^{x} + e^{y}\right) = -e^{x}\)

\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^{y}}{-e^{x}} = -\frac{e^{y}}{e^{x}}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -e^{y - x}\), as required.
twin: If \(e^x + e^y = e^{x+y}\), then show that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -e^{y-x}\).

**(D)** \(\frac{1}{2}\)

By the rule for the derivative of an inverse function, \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(b) = \frac{1}{f'(a)}\), where \(f(a) = b\). So first find the \(x\) that \(f\) sends to \(-3\).

Given: \(f(x) = x^{5} + 2x - 3\)
Put \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 0 + 0 - 3 = -3\), so \(a = 0\).
(This is the only such \(x\), since \(f'(x) = 5x^{4} + 2 > 0\) makes \(f\) strictly increasing, hence one-one.)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
\(f'(x) = 5x^{4} + 2\)
\(\therefore f'(0) = 5(0) + 2 = 2\)

\(\therefore \left(f^{-1}\right)'(-3) = \frac{1}{f'(0)} = \frac{1}{2}\)

Given: \(y = \cos\left(m\cos^{-1}x\right)\)
\(\therefore \cos^{-1}y = m\cos^{-1}x\) ... (I)

Differentiate (I) w. r. t. \(x\),
\(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{m}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\)
\(\therefore \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} = m\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}\)

Square both sides — this clears both radicals, which is what makes a second differentiation possible,
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2} = m^{2}\left(1 - y^{2}\right)\)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\) (product rule on the left, chain rule on the right),
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\cdot 2\frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}(-2x) = m^{2}(-2y)\frac{dy}{dx}\)

Divide throughout by \(2\frac{dy}{dx}\),
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} - x\frac{dy}{dx} = -m^{2}y\)
\(\therefore \left(1 - x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} - x\frac{dy}{dx} + m^{2}y = 0\), as required.

[Verified independently: computing \(y_{1}\) and \(y_{2}\) from \(y = \cos(m\cos^{-1}x)\) and substituting makes the left side vanish identically.]
twin: If \(y = \cos (m \cos^{-1} x)\) then show that \((1 - x^2) \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - x \frac{dy}{dx} + m^2 y = 0\).

answer:
Given: \(y = \sin^{-1}x\), \(|x| < 1\)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\)
\(\therefore \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\)

Square both sides to remove the radical,
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2} = 1\)

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\), using the product rule on the left,
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\cdot 2\frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}(-2x) = 0\)

Divide throughout by \(2\frac{dy}{dx}\), which is non-zero since \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} > 0\),
\(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} - x\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), as required.

[Cross-check by direct computation: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{-1/2}\) and \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = x\left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{-3/2}\), so \(\left(1 - x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = x\left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{-1/2} = x\frac{dy}{dx}\).]
twin: If \(y = \cos (m \cos^{-1} x)\) then show that \((1 - x^2) \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - x \frac{dy}{dx} + m^2 y = 0\).

answer:
Let \(y = \log x\), \(x > 0\).

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} = x^{-1}\)

Differentiate again,
\(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = -x^{-2} = \frac{(-1)^{1}\cdot 1}{x^{2}}\)

Again,
\(\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}} = (-1)(-2)x^{-3} = \frac{(-1)^{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2}{x^{3}}\)

Again,
\(\frac{d^{4}y}{dx^{4}} = \frac{(-1)^{3}\cdot 1\cdot 2\cdot 3}{x^{4}}\)

The pattern is now clear: each differentiation flips the sign and multiplies the numerator by the next integer, while the power of \(x\) in the denominator goes up by one. In general, the \(n^{th}\) order derivative is
\(\frac{d^{n}y}{dx^{n}} = \frac{(-1)^{n - 1}\cdot 1\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdots(n - 1)}{x^{n}}\)
\(\therefore \frac{d^{n}y}{dx^{n}} = \frac{(-1)^{n - 1}(n - 1)!}{x^{n}}\)

Check at \(n = 4\): \(\frac{(-1)^{3}\cdot 3!}{x^{4}} = -\frac{6}{x^{4}}\), which matches the fourth derivative computed above.

**(B)** \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)

To differentiate one function with respect to another, differentiate each with respect to the common variable \(\theta\) and divide.

Let \(u = \tan^{3}\theta\) and \(v = \sec^{3}\theta\); we need \(\frac{du}{dv}\).
\(\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{du/d\theta}{dv/d\theta}\) ... (I)

Now \(u = \tan^{3}\theta\), so
\(\frac{du}{d\theta} = 3\tan^{2}\theta\cdot\frac{d}{d\theta}(\tan\theta) = 3\tan^{2}\theta\sec^{2}\theta\) ... (II)

And \(v = \sec^{3}\theta\), so
\(\frac{dv}{d\theta} = 3\sec^{2}\theta\cdot\frac{d}{d\theta}(\sec\theta) = 3\sec^{2}\theta\cdot\sec\theta\tan\theta = 3\sec^{3}\theta\tan\theta\) ... (III)

Substituting (II) and (III) in (I),
\(\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{3\tan^{2}\theta\sec^{2}\theta}{3\sec^{3}\theta\tan\theta} = \frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta} = \sin\theta\)

At \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\),
\(\left(\frac{du}{dv}\right)_{\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}} = \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)

[Option (D) is the same value with a sign error; nothing in the working produces a negative, since \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} > 0\).]

To prove: if \(y = f(u)\) is a differentiable function of \(u\) and \(u = g(x)\) is a differentiable function of \(x\), then \(y = f[g(x)]\) is a differentiable function of \(x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\).

Proof:
Let \(\delta x\) be a small increment in \(x\), \(\delta x \neq 0\). Let \(\delta u\) be the corresponding increment in \(u\) and \(\delta y\) the corresponding increment in \(y\).

Since \(u = g(x)\) is differentiable it is continuous, so
\(\delta u \rightarrow 0\) as \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\).

Assume \(\delta u \neq 0\) for all sufficiently small \(\delta x \neq 0\). (This is the assumption the standard proof makes; it is stated here rather than hidden.) Then we may write
\(\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \frac{\delta y}{\delta u}\times\frac{\delta u}{\delta x}\)

Taking limits as \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\), and noting that \(\delta u \rightarrow 0\) as \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\),
\(\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \lim_{\delta u \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta u}\times\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta u}{\delta x}\)

Now \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(u\), so \(\lim_{\delta u \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta u} = \frac{dy}{du}\) exists; and \(u\) is a differentiable function of \(x\), so \(\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta u}{\delta x} = \frac{du}{dx}\) exists.

Both limits on the right exist, so the limit on the left exists; that is, \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(x\), and
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\)

Hence proved. (This is the chain rule.)

[The stem prints "prove that \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(y\)"; it should read "\(x\) is a differentiable function of \(y\)", which is what the stated conclusion \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{dy/dx}\) is about. Proved in that sense below.]

To prove: if \(y = f(x)\) is a differentiable function of \(x\) such that the inverse function \(x = f^{-1}(y)\) exists, then \(x\) is a differentiable function of \(y\) and \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{\frac{dy}{dx}}\), where \(\frac{dy}{dx} \neq 0\).

Proof:
Let \(\delta x\) be a small increment in \(x\), \(\delta x \neq 0\), and let \(\delta y\) be the corresponding increment in \(y\).

Since \(f^{-1}\) exists, \(f\) is one-one, so \(\delta x \neq 0\) forces \(\delta y \neq 0\); and since \(f\) is differentiable it is continuous, so \(\delta y \rightarrow 0\) as \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\).

As \(\delta y \neq 0\) and \(\delta x \neq 0\),
\(\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}\times\frac{\delta x}{\delta y} = 1\)
\(\therefore \frac{\delta x}{\delta y} = \frac{1}{\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}}\)

Taking limits as \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\) (so that \(\delta y \rightarrow 0\)),
\(\lim_{\delta y \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta x}{\delta y} = \frac{1}{\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}} = \frac{1}{\frac{dy}{dx}}\), which exists because \(\frac{dy}{dx} \neq 0\).

Hence \(x\) is a differentiable function of \(y\) and
\(\therefore \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{\frac{dy}{dx}}\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} \neq 0\).

Hence find \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}x\right)\):
Let \(y = \tan^{-1}x\), \(-\frac{\pi}{2} < y < \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Then \(x = \tan y\).
Differentiate w. r. t. \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy} = \sec^{2}y = 1 + \tan^{2}y = 1 + x^{2}\)
Since \(1 + x^{2} \neq 0\), by the rule just proved,
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\frac{dx}{dy}} = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\)
\(\therefore \frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}x\right) = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\)

To prove: if \(x = f(t)\) and \(y = g(t)\) are differentiable functions of \(t\), then \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), where \(\frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0\).

Proof:
Let \(\delta t\) be a small increment in \(t\), \(\delta t \neq 0\). Let \(\delta x\) and \(\delta y\) be the corresponding increments in \(x\) and \(y\).

Since \(x\) and \(y\) are differentiable functions of \(t\) they are continuous, so \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\) and \(\delta y \rightarrow 0\) as \(\delta t \rightarrow 0\).

As \(\frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0\), we have \(\delta x \neq 0\) for all sufficiently small \(\delta t \neq 0\), and so
\(\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \frac{\frac{\delta y}{\delta t}}{\frac{\delta x}{\delta t}}\)

Taking limits as \(\delta t \rightarrow 0\) (equivalently \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\)), and using the limit of a quotient,
\(\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \frac{\lim_{\delta t \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta t}}{\lim_{\delta t \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta x}{\delta t}}\)

Both limits on the right exist and the denominator \(\frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0\), so the limit on the left exists; that is, \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(x\), and
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}}\)

Hence find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) if \(x = a\cos^{2}t\) and \(y = a\sin^{2}t\):
\(x = a\cos^{2}t\)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(t\),
\(\frac{dx}{dt} = a\cdot 2\cos t\cdot(-\sin t) = -2a\sin t\cos t = -a\sin 2t\) ... (I)

\(y = a\sin^{2}t\)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(t\),
\(\frac{dy}{dt} = a\cdot 2\sin t\cdot\cos t = a\sin 2t\) ... (II)

From (I) and (II), for \(\sin 2t \neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{a\sin 2t}{-a\sin 2t}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -1\)

Check: \(x + y = a\cos^{2}t + a\sin^{2}t = a\), a constant, so the point traces part of the line \(x + y = a\), whose slope is indeed \(-1\).

The identity exactly as printed is false — see the errata note. What follows proves the correct second-order identity for the same function, which is what the question is testing, and then demonstrates that the printed form does not hold.

\(y = e^{m\tan^{-1}x}\)

**Step 1 — first derivative.** By the chain rule, with \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\),

\(y_{1} = \dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{m\tan^{-1}x} \cdot \dfrac{m}{1 + x^{2}} = \dfrac{my}{1 + x^{2}}\)

**Step 2 — clear the denominator before differentiating again.** This is the step that keeps the second differentiation clean:

\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)y_{1} = my\)   ...(i)

**Step 3 — differentiate (i) with respect to \(x\)**, using the product rule on the left:

\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)y_{2} + 2x\,y_{1} = m\,y_{1}\)

\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)y_{2} + 2x\,y_{1} - m\,y_{1} = 0\)

\(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)y_{2} + (2x - m)y_{1} = 0\)   ...(ii)

which is the required result.

**Verification at \(m = 1,\ x = 0\).** There \(y = e^{0} = 1\) and \(y_{1} = \dfrac{1 \times 1}{1 + 0} = 1\). Differentiating \(y_{1} = \dfrac{my}{1 + x^{2}}\) by the quotient rule,

\(y_{2} = \dfrac{m\,y_{1}\left(1 + x^{2}\right) - my(2x)}{\left(1 + x^{2}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{1 \times 1 \times 1 - 0}{1} = 1\)

Correct form (ii): \(\left(1\right)(1) + \left(0 - 1\right)(1) = 1 - 1 = 0\) — the identity holds.

Printed form: \(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2} + (2x - 2m)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (1)(1)^{2} + (0 - 2)(1) = 1 - 2 = -1 \neq 0\) — the identity fails.

Proof:
Let \(\delta t\) be a small increment in \(t\), \(\delta t \neq 0\), and let \(\delta x\), \(\delta y\) be the corresponding increments in \(x\) and \(y\).

Since \(x\) and \(y\) are differentiable functions of \(t\) they are continuous, so \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\) and \(\delta y \rightarrow 0\) as \(\delta t \rightarrow 0\).

\(\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \frac{\frac{\delta y}{\delta t}}{\frac{\delta x}{\delta t}}\)

Taking limits as \(\delta t \rightarrow 0\) (equivalently \(\delta x \rightarrow 0\)),
\(\lim_{\delta x \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \frac{\lim_{\delta t \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta y}{\delta t}}{\lim_{\delta t \rightarrow 0}\frac{\delta x}{\delta t}}\)

Both limits on the right exist and the denominator is non-zero, so
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}}\)

Hence find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) if \(x = \sin t\) and \(y = \cos t\):
\(x = \sin t\)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(t\),
\(\frac{dx}{dt} = \cos t\) ... (I)

\(y = \cos t\)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(t\),
\(\frac{dy}{dt} = -\sin t\) ... (II)

From (I) and (II), for \(\cos t \neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-\sin t}{\cos t}\)
\(\therefore \frac{dy}{dx} = -\tan t\)

Check: \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\), the unit circle; differentiating that implicitly gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y} = -\frac{\sin t}{\cos t} = -\tan t\), the same answer.

Hence find the derivative of \(7^{x}\) w. r. t. \(x^{7}\):
Here the common variable is \(x\) itself, so the rule just proved reads \(\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{du/dx}{dv/dx}\).

Let \(u = 7^{x}\) and \(v = x^{7}\); we need \(\frac{du}{dv}\).
\(\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{\frac{du}{dx}}{\frac{dv}{dx}}\) ... (I)

Now \(u = 7^{x}\)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),

Differentiate w. r. t. \(x\),
